title: DFA or NFA?
subtitle: 15 graph-classification questions
instructions: Use the complete-DFA convention: exactly one destination per state and input symbol, with no ε-transitions. Choose NFA for branching or ε-NFA graphs. A double circle marks an accepting state; it does not by itself imply nondeterminism.

questions.prompt: Alphabet Σ={0, 1}. Is this graph a DFA or an NFA?
questions.explanation: Every state has exactly one destination for each symbol in Σ={0, 1} and there are no ε-transitions. The number of accepting states and unreachable states does not change determinism.

questions.prompt: Alphabet Σ={0, 1}. Is this graph a DFA or an NFA?
questions.explanation: At q0, symbol 0 can reach {q0, q1}. That gives multiple destinations for the same state–symbol pair, so this is an NFA, not a DFA.

questions.prompt: Alphabet Σ={a, b}. Is this graph a DFA or an NFA?
questions.explanation: Every state has exactly one destination for each symbol in Σ={a, b} and there are no ε-transitions. The number of accepting states and unreachable states does not change determinism.

title: Can this DFA be reduced?
subtitle: 15 graph-minimization questions
instructions: All figures in this quiz are complete DFAs. Answer Yes only if the equivalent DFA can have fewer states. Check both unreachable states and equivalent reachable states. Minimizing an already-minimal DFA does not reduce its state count.

questions.prompt: Can this DFA be reduced to fewer states without changing its accepted language?
choices: Yes — it can be reduced further
questions.explanation: Yes. Merge equivalent states {p, r}: they have the same accept/reject behavior for every continuation. This reduces 3 states to 2.

questions.prompt: Can this DFA be reduced to fewer states without changing its accepted language?
choices: Yes — it can be reduced further
questions.explanation: No. All states are reachable, and the stable equivalence classes are {e} | {o}. Every pair is distinguishable, so no merge preserves the language. The minimum remains 2 states.
